prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

A hundred and one butter lamps are offered to my uncle who is no more. Distraction proves fatal in death. A curtain of butter imprints in air. After the burning of bones, ashes are sent on pilgrimage. You are dead, go into life, we pray. My uncle was a man given to giggles in solemn moments. Memory springs like crocuses in bloom. Self conscious and precise. Without blurring the cornea, details are resuscitated. Dried yak meat between teeth. Semblance of what is. Do not be distracted, Uncle who is no more. He does not see his reflection in the river. The arching of speech over “s” as he is becoming. Curvature of spine as it cracked on a misty morning. A shadow evades the wall. You are no more, Uncle who is no more. Every seven days he must relive his moment of expiration. The living pray frequently amid burning juniper. Communication efforts require the right initiative. Somewhere along the line matters of motion and rest are resolved. Crows pick the last offerings. You are someone else, uncle no more.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Distraction, After, You

outputs.L1:
One hundred and one butter lamps are offered to my uncle, who is no more. Distraction proves fatal in death. A curtain of butter leaves its imprint upon the air. After the bones have burned, the ashes are sent on pilgrimage. *You are dead; go into life,* we pray.

My uncle was a man prone to giggling in solemn moments. Memory springs forth like crocuses in bloom—self-conscious and precise. Without clouding the cornea, details are resuscitated: dried yak meat caught between the teeth, a semblance of what is.

Do not be distracted, Uncle who is no more. He does not see his reflection in the river. The arching of speech over the letter “s” as he is becoming. The curvature of his spine as it cracked on a misty morning. A shadow evades the wall.

You are no more, Uncle who is no more. Every seven days, he must relive the moment of his expiration. Amid burning juniper, the living pray frequently. Efforts at communication require the right initiative. Somewhere along the way, matters of motion and rest are resolved. Crows pick at the last offerings.

You are someone else, Uncle no more.
outputs.L2:
For my departed uncle, we light and present 101 lamps filled with butter. In the realm of death, losing focus can be ruinous. The smoke hangs like a veil, carrying the marks of butter through the air. Once his bones have been cremated, the remaining ash is taken on a sacred journey. Our prayer is this: though you have died, enter life.

My uncle often giggled when occasions demanded seriousness. Recollections emerge suddenly, like flowering crocuses—careful, exact, and aware of themselves. The eye remains clear as particulars return to life: strips of dried yak flesh caught between his teeth, faint likenesses of what once existed. Departed uncle, do not let your attention wander.

The river gives him no image of himself. As he comes into another state of being, his voice curves around the letter “s.” I remember the bend of his back when it broke one fog-laden morning. His shadow slips away from the wall. You have ceased to exist, my uncle who has gone.

At intervals of seven days, he is compelled to experience the instant of his death again. Those still alive pray repeatedly while juniper burns around them. Reaching across the divide depends on beginning in the proper way. At some point, the questions of stillness and movement find their answer. Crows arrive to consume what remains of the offerings. You have become another being; you are no longer my uncle.
outputs.L3:
The speaker offers 101 butter lamps and prayers to help guide a deceased uncle from death toward a new life. This spiritual act is also deeply personal, as the uncle is remembered through vivid and affectionate details: his solemn giggles, his precise manner, the distinctive qualities of his speech and posture, and even his eating habits. These memories preserve him as a recognizable individual while emphasizing the intimacy of the speaker’s grief.

At the same time, rituals such as burning the uncle’s bones, sending his ashes on pilgrimage, and burning juniper create a connection between the living and the dead. They allow the family to honor him while supporting his passage through a spiritual transition. The poem repeatedly warns the uncle not to become distracted as he confronts the reality of his death and moves toward rebirth. Ultimately, however, the familiar person recalled by the speaker cannot remain unchanged. By the end of the poem, the uncle’s former identity begins to dissolve, suggesting that death and rebirth transform him into someone entirely new.
outputs.L4:
The poem is an elegy for a deceased uncle, shaped by the beliefs and practices of Tibetan Buddhism. Rather than presenting death as a sudden ending, it depicts it as a passage through ritual, memory, and spiritual transformation. The speaker’s grief unfolds alongside prayers, offerings, cremation rites, and images of rebirth, suggesting that the uncle’s consciousness must be guided away from earthly attachments and toward a new existence.

Sensory memories keep the uncle vividly present. Sounds, smells, textures, and visual details connect the solemnity of the rituals to the speaker’s personal recollections of him. These concrete impressions make grief feel immediate and physical: although the uncle has died, he survives in remembered gestures, familiar objects, and the atmosphere surrounding the ceremonies. Repetition reinforces this tension between presence and absence. Recurring words and images resemble both the circular movement of mourning and the repeated chanting of prayer, as if language itself could accompany the dead on his journey.

The poem’s surreal imagery further blurs the boundaries between the material and spiritual worlds. Offerings may appear to change form, smoke from the cremation may merge with prayer or landscape, and the uncle’s body may seem to dissolve into elements that can be carried elsewhere. Such transformations express a Buddhist understanding of impermanence: the body cannot remain, but death does not necessarily mean annihilation. Instead, cremation becomes both destruction and release, while prayers help direct the deceased through the uncertain interval between one life and the next.

At the same time, the rituals serve the living as much as they serve the dead. By preparing offerings, repeating prayers, and observing the body’s return to the elements, the mourners give structure to an experience that might otherwise seem unbearable. Remembrance initially holds the uncle close, but the poem gradually recognizes that love cannot depend on possession. To guide him onward, the family must loosen its attachment and accept change.

The poem therefore presents mourning as a double movement: the dead are encouraged toward rebirth, while the living move from grief toward acceptance. Memory does not prevent this release; instead, it makes release possible by honoring what has been lost. Through ritual, repetition, and visionary images, sorrow is transformed into an act of care. The uncle is not forgotten, but neither is he confined to the past. He is remembered, blessed, and finally allowed to continue into another form of existence.
outputs.L5:
**After You**

Distraction arrived quietly, disguised as routine. A cup left beside the sink. A song playing from another room. A message I almost sent.

After you, the world continued with astonishing confidence. Traffic lights changed, strangers laughed, and rain gathered along the windows. Everything moved forward except the part of me still waiting at the door.

I filled my days with noise, hoping distraction might become healing. But every silence led back to you.

And perhaps that is what “after” truly means—not forgetting, but learning to carry the memory without letting it choose the way.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a lyrical prose poem about a Tibetan Buddhist funeral ritual for a deceased uncle, incorporating butter lamps, cremation ashes, juniper smoke, recurring prayers, and the soul’s passage into another life.
counterfactuals.output:
At dawn we carried Uncle’s name into the shrine room, where butter lamps trembled in their brass bowls, each flame a small golden door. Outside, the mountains stood silent beneath their shawls of snow. Inside, juniper branches hissed upon the coals, and their blue smoke climbed the rafters, carrying the fragrance of earth, winter, and farewell.

The prayers began, ended, and began again. Their syllables moved like prayer wheels turned by an unseen hand—round and round, wearing a path through grief. We whispered them for the loosening of fear, for clear light in the dark interval, for the traveler who no longer wore Uncle’s face.

Later, we gathered his cremation ashes: pale fragments, quiet as dust after snowfall. How little remained of the hands that had mended bridles, poured tea, lifted children onto his shoulders. Yet the lamas reminded us that nothing truly stays, and nothing simply vanishes. Smoke becomes sky; snow becomes river; one life leans toward another.

So we fed the butter lamps and watched their flames bow without going out. Juniper smoke drifted across the valley. Again the prayers returned, steady as footsteps: go gently, go without clinging, recognize the light before you.

And what we called his soul—his bright, wandering consciousness—passed beyond the reach of our voices, bearing their echo toward another mother, another morning, another body opening its eyes beneath the vast and turning sky.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose an experimental elegy for an uncle who has died. Use fragmented, surreal imagery and repeat variations of the phrase “Uncle who is no more.”
counterfactuals.output:
**Elegy with Missing Door**

Uncle who is no more,  
your coat still hangs  
from the shoulder of the hallway.

In its pockets:  
three nails,  
a receipt for rain,  
the blue tooth of a clock.

*

Uncle who is no longer—  
the kitchen keeps mispronouncing your name.  
Spoon against cup.  
Pipe against wall.  
A small metallic weather.

You have gone where the radio goes  
after the song:  
into wheat-static,  
into the white field  
behind hearing.

*

O uncle who is no more,  
the moon has borrowed your hands.

Tonight it repairs nothing.

The fence leans inward.  
The apples dream of falling  
but wake among roots.  
Your chair grows lighter  
and lighter—  
a wooden bird refusing flight.

*

Uncle who was,  
uncle who is ash now,  
uncle translated into closed curtains—

I remember your laugh:  
a jar breaking  
in a room full of summer.

Or was it thunder  
wearing your old boots?

*

Uncle who is no more,  
we set a plate for absence.  
Absence eats slowly.  
Absence asks for salt.

Under the table,  
the dog listens  
to the country of the dead  
ticking inside the floorboards.

*

No-more uncle,  
un-uncle,  
dear torn page—

your face drifts through the family photographs  
like a pale animal under ice.

We point.  
We say *there*.  
But there has already become  
another word for nowhere.

*

Uncle who is no more,  
I carry your name in my mouth  
like a key  
to a house that has forgotten its doors.

Still, some nights,  
the dark coughs once—

and every window  
turns toward it.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a prose poem exploring grief, memory, and reincarnation through precise sensory details such as dried yak meat, crows eating offerings, a river without a reflection, and 101 butter lamps.
counterfactuals.output:
After you died, the kitchen kept your weather: smoke caught in the rafters, salt on the sill, dried yak meat hanging from a blackened beam, hard as bark beneath my thumb. I cut it thin and chewed until the old hunger returned—the one that belonged to winter, when you warmed my boots beside the stove and said the body is only a room the wind rents.

At dawn I carried barley, tea, and apricots to the ridge. Crows were eating the offerings before I finished arranging them, their beaks bright with butter, their wings folding and unfolding like scorched letters. I wanted to drive them away, but remembered how you laughed: Let the dead choose their mouths. One crow looked at me with your impatient eye, then lifted into the cold, dropping a grain that vanished in the grass.

Below, the river ran without a reflection. Mountains leaned over it and found nothing; clouds passed across its surface without entering. I knelt and searched for my face, then yours, but the water kept only the taste of iron and snow. When I touched it, my fingers ached as if gripping the hand you withdrew from mine.

That evening I lit 101 butter lamps. Their wicks hissed softly, each flame bending toward the next, a procession of small golden lives. The room smelled of milk, soot, and the wool of your old coat. I named what I could remember: the scar on your wrist, juniper crushed beneath your heel, the blue cup chipped at the rim, your breath sweetened by fennel. I named what I had already lost: the exact weight of your head on my shoulder, the last word you spoke, whether the door closed before or after the rain began.

By midnight, the lamps had become a field of trembling suns. A moth circled them, singed itself, vanished into darkness, returned. I understood then that grief is not a road away from the dead. It is the dark that teaches light to come back differently. Perhaps you are already near—feather, river-cold, a child waking with salt on her tongue, astonished by the smell of smoke. Perhaps I, too, have carried you before, in another kitchen, under another name.

One by one, the flames lowered into the butter. I did not say goodbye. I opened the window. Outside, the crows slept with their black heads beneath their wings, and somewhere beyond the moonless ridge, water hurried on, bearing no face, refusing no return.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a meditative literary passage in which a speaker remembers a giggling uncle during the forty-nine days after his death, blending intimate physical memories with Buddhist beliefs about the intermediate state.
counterfactuals.output:
For forty-nine days, we kept a lamp burning beside his photograph.

In it, Uncle was laughing too hard to be still. His head tipped back, eyes narrowed to shining seams, one hand caught in the blur of slapping his knee. I could almost hear the giggle that always escaped before the real laughter—a high, mischievous sound, astonishing in a man with such broad shoulders and solemn gray eyebrows.

The teachings say that after death the mind wanders an intermediate country, meeting its own radiance and fear. Every seven days, we read prayers aloud, asking him to recognize whatever appeared: Do not be afraid of the bright light. Do not cling to the dim one. Remember that every terror is your own mind. Remember that you are dead.

But I remembered his body.

The roughness of his cheek when he bent to greet me. The medicinal sweetness of the oil he rubbed into his knees. The small crescent scar beside his thumb, pale as a new moon. How, when I was a child, he let me stand on his feet and walked me across the room, my soles resting on the warm leather of his shoes. Left, right, left—his hands enclosing mine, his giggle trembling through his chest.

On the fourteenth day, I dreamed he was looking for his glasses. On the twenty-first, a moth circled the lamp and struck the shade with a papery tap. My aunt whispered his name. None of us said we believed it was him, but we opened the window.

As the weeks passed, grief changed texture. At first it was a stone lodged behind the breastbone. Later it became water, entering everything without shape: the folded towel in his bathroom, the cup with a brown seam of tea, a single white hair caught in the teeth of his comb. I began to understand why the prayers spoke so often of attachment. Love, too, has hands. It grasps the sleeve. It calls the traveler back.

On the forty-ninth morning, we offered rice, fruit, incense, and the merit of every kindness we could remember. I offered the afternoon he taught me to whistle through a blade of grass, though I never managed it. I offered the times he laughed before reaching the end of his own joke. I offered the weight of his palm on my head.

The smoke rose and loosened.

If he was still between worlds, I wanted him to hear us. If he had already entered another life, I wanted some infant, somewhere, to wake from sleep with that giggle bubbling inexplicably in its throat.

Then the lamp went out—not suddenly, but with a last blue bow of flame.

I did not relight it.

I sat in the faint smell of smoke and felt, for one impossible instant, his large warm hand closing over mine—not holding, exactly, but teaching it how to open.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a haunting, nonlinear elegy set amid Himalayan death rites. Contrast the dead uncle’s distinctive gestures and mannerisms with cremation, weekly rituals, distraction after death, and his eventual transformation into someone else.
counterfactuals.output:
### **After the Snow Took Your Name**

By the seventh Saturday  
we had learned to leave rice  
where your hands were not.

The priest rang a bell into the wind.  
Juniper smoke climbed the blue ravine,  
lost its way among the prayer flags.  
A crow tilted its head—  
the exact impatient angle  
you used when tea was too sweet.

But you were already burning.

No—first you were laughing,  
thumb polishing the brass head of your cane,  
one eyelid closing before the joke arrived.  
First you tucked your lower lip beneath your teeth  
to count money.  
First you entered every room sideways,  
as though apologizing to the air  
for having a body.

Then the ghat stones, river-cold.  
Then ghee, sandalwood, the eldest nephew’s torch.  
Your left foot, always restless at meals,  
stood briefly out from the pyre  
like a road refusing its mountain.

Someone pushed it back.

Weeks moved without sequence.  
On Tuesdays we fed the flame.  
On Saturdays we fed the absent.  
Barley flour, black sesame, water poured  
through a ring of grass—  
small provisions for the long, unmapped country.

Between rites, we became ordinary.

Your brother argued over bus fare.  
Your widow watched a serial too loudly.  
I answered messages beside your photograph  
while the butter lamp worried itself thin.  
Children chased a punctured ball  
through the courtyard where mourners  
had once whispered your virtues.

Grief, insulted, went outside  
and sat among the nettles.

Much later—earlier—  
your ashes entered the river.  
The river did not pause.  
It carried your knuckles, your cataract,  
the mole below your ear,  
the little cough you placed before disagreement,  
down through ice-light and silt.

We kept only your gestures,  
and even these betrayed you.

Your widow began closing one eye before laughing.  
Your brother tapped the table twice  
before lifting his cup.  
A niece, born after the smoke,  
entered rooms sideways.

Everyone said, Look.

Everyone said, He has returned.

But the child disliked tea.  
She feared crows.  
She took your cane in both hands  
and struck the prayer wheel  
until all its prayers flew loose.

By the forty-ninth day—  
or by the first, or by the winter  
before your death—  
your photograph had become a photograph  
of someone we had loved correctly.

The mountain accepted no correction.

Snow filled the cremation ground,  
softening the black stones,  
covering the place where your foot  
had resisted.

And you, Uncle—  
freed from your cough, your sideways entrance,  
your thumb circling brass—  
became first smoke,

then ritual,

then interruption,

then the child in the courtyard  
turning at the sound of a name  
that was no longer yours.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
